title: Compliance
sequence: Business Environment topic. Compliance requirements are confirmed at the start of planning and rechecked whenever scope, jurisdiction, product or rules change; compliance is verified throughout and at closure.

header.html: Business Environment domain (26%) · Task 2 Plan and manage project compliance — confirm project compliance requirements (e.g., security, health and safety, sustainability, regulatory compliance) · classify compliance categories · determine potential threats to compliance · use methods to support compliance · analyze the consequences of noncompliance · determine the necessary approach and action(s) to address compliance needs · measure the extent to which the project is in compliance

Topic 06 (ethics and policies) · Topic 07 (sustainability requirements) · Topic 12 (governance and OPAs) · Topic 18 (quality and regulatory compliance) · Topic 21 (compliance threats are risks) · Topic 22 (supplier compliance, contract clauses) · Topic 29 (change control) · Topic 33 (changes in the external environment) · Topic 35 (verify obligations at closure)

Standard §1.3 and §2.2 (organizational governance enforces legal, regulatory and compliance requirements; enterprise environmental factors such as legal restrictions, government and industry standards, public health and safety regulations; OPAs) · Governance domain (ensure compliance with regulatory and legal requirements; Table 2-5 compliance audits and checklists; multinational compliance example; metric "compliance with corporate and legal policies") · Manage Quality Assurance (regulations, compliance, audits) · Close Project or Phase (verify that all contractual, regulatory, legal, social and environmental obligations have been met) · Standard §3.7 (sustainability and compliance-oriented project management) · Finance tailoring (SOX, GDPR) · Appendix X3 (AI privacy and legal regulations)

PMBOK 8 has no dedicated compliance process. The enablers are built from governance, EEF/OPA, quality assurance and risk material plus common exam practice, so much of the structure here is tagged [Beyond PMBOK 8].

[Beyond PMBOK 8] = exam-relevant, but PMBOK 8 does not spell it out (ECO wording, common exam practice, mock-exam style).

toc.title: Determine the Necessary Approach and Actions (ECO)
Measure the Extent to Which the Project Is Compliant (ECO)
Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

html:
1Core Concepts and Definitions

Term Meaning
Compliance Meeting the requirements the project is bound by: laws and regulations, standards, contractual terms, and organizational policies
Regulations Requirements imposed by a governmental body that can set product, process or service characteristics, including administrative provisions with government-mandated compliance
Standard A document established by an authority, custom or general consent as a model or example
Compliance requirement A specific obligation the project must meet (a rule, control, report, certification, approval, test or record)
Mandatory vs voluntary Beyond PMBOK 8 Mandatory: law, regulation, contract. Voluntary: optional standards or good practice, adopted by decision
Threat to compliance A condition or event that could cause the project to fail a compliance requirement; managed as a risk until it occurs, then as an issue
Compliance evidence Records that prove compliance: test results, audit reports, approvals, permits, logs, certificates
Compliance-oriented project management PMBOK 8's narrowest orientation (conform to rules); sustainability broadens the orientation toward achievement and society (Standard Figure 3-8)
Organizational governance Direction and control through policies and decisions; enforces legal, regulatory and compliance requirements and defines ethical, social and environmental responsibilities

2Where Compliance Requirements Come From

Source Examples (PMBOK 8)
EEFs: legal restrictions Country or local laws and regulations on security, data protection, business conduct, employment and procurement
EEFs: government or industry standards Regulatory agency regulations and standards on products, production, environment, safety, quality and workmanship
EEFs: public health and safety regulations Government-imposed health protocols, travel restrictions, quarantine, public safety mandates
EEFs: other Financial rules (taxes, tariffs), geopolitical constraints, emerging-technology rules (AI privacy)
OPAs Organizational policies, procedures, templates, regulations the organization has adopted, lessons learned
Contracts and agreements Customer and supplier terms, SLAs, acceptance criteria, flow-down clauses
Sponsor, customer and stakeholder commitments Sustainability KPIs written into the charter, business case, scope statement or contracts; customer-specific standards, which may be stricter than regulators'

Governance ensures compliance with regulatory and legal requirements to maintain organizational accountability; a project may even be terminated for legal, regulatory or compliance reasons (Standard).

3Confirm Compliance Requirements (ECO)

  • Identify what applies by jurisdiction, industry, product, substance, data type, technology, location and market. Do not assume the rules you know apply to something new (a new market, material, data store or technology).
  • Consult the experts: legal and compliance functions, subject matter experts, regulators and certifying bodies; review contracts; check organizational policies.
  • Confirm with the sponsor and governance which obligations are mandatory, which are voluntary and who is accountable.
  • Record them where work gets planned: requirements documentation and traceability matrix, quality requirements and acceptance criteria, the WBS or backlog, schedule (permits, approvals, inspections), budget, and assumption log.
  • Do it early, before design, procurement or market entry; reconfirm when scope, location, supplier or technology changes.
  • Examples of fast-changing situations: a new regulation that takes effect in three months (confirm its requirements and prioritize them in the backlog); data about children or health (check residency and privacy obligations before choosing storage); a restricted ingredient in one export market (determine the compliance approach before launch); a new substance (determine which regulations apply, do not borrow those of the old one).

4Classify Compliance Categories (ECO)

Why classify: each category has different owners, experts, evidence and risk. Classification also separates mandatory from voluntary and shows priority by consequence and deadline. Beyond PMBOK 8the category list is a study aid

Category Typical examples Typical evidence
Legal and regulatory Product, industry and market laws; employment, procurement, trade, sanctions Legal opinion, permits, licenses
Security and privacy Data protection and residency, information security, AI and privacy rules Security tests, access logs, assessments
Health and safety Workplace safety, public health protocols, infection control Inspections, safety plans, incident records
Environmental and sustainability Emissions, energy, water, waste, ESG commitments Measurements, certifications, reports
Quality and industry standards Product and process standards, certifications, accessibility Tests, audits, certificates
Financial and reporting Financial controls and data integrity (SOX-type), tax, statutory reporting Control tests, audit trails
Contractual SLAs, acceptance criteria, flow-down clauses Compliance matrix, acceptance records
Organizational policy and ethics Code of conduct, gifts and conflicts of interest, approval rules Ethics reviews, approvals, training records

5Determine Potential Threats to Compliance (ECO)

Threat source Examples
Change in rules New or amended regulation, new standard version, changed interpretation, geopolitical or sanctions changes (Topic 33)
Change in the project New market or jurisdiction, new substance, supplier or technology, scope or design changes, reuse of data
Third parties A supplier or contractor that does not meet requirements (a plan that omits required infection control, staff without certification, data processing abroad)
Knowledge and behavior Gaps in awareness or training; shortcuts under schedule pressure; gifts and conflicts of interest
Evidence and records Missing documentation, uncontrolled files, approved versions that cannot be found
Technology Known security weaknesses, unvetted AI tools processing confidential or personal data
Jurisdictional differences Multinational projects must follow different regional rules; variations may need program- or portfolio-level governance
Timing Permit or approval delays; deadlines for new rules
  • Treat threats as risks: register them with an owner and a response; known weaknesses need an exposure-reducing response (insurance does not protect data; Topic 21).
  • When a threat occurs (for example an announced permit backlog), it becomes an issue: log it, execute the planned response, update the register and inform stakeholders (Topic 30).

6Analyze the Consequences of Noncompliance (ECO)

Consequences to analyze [Beyond PMBOK 8: grouping]: harm to people or the environment; stop-work orders or loss of license to operate; project termination; fines and penalties; legal action and personal liability; contract termination or penalties; rework and delay (fixing later costs more); loss of market access; reputation damage and stakeholder dissatisfaction.

  • Assess likelihood and impact (Topic 21) and who is affected (customers, public, regulators, team).
  • Compare the cost of compliance with the cost of noncompliance, as with cost of quality. For mandatory requirements the question is how, not whether.
  • Show the analysis to the sponsor and governance before anyone proposes cutting a corner. If a deadline conflicts with a mandatory requirement, present the consequences and schedule-safe alternatives.
  • Document the analysis; it supports decisions, audits and escalation.

7Determine the Necessary Approach and Actions (ECO)

Situation Approach
Mandatory requirement Build it in: add to scope, WBS or backlog, schedule, budget and definition of done or phase exit criteria; assign an owner; plan how compliance will be verified and evidenced; train; monitor
Voluntary standard or policy Evaluate value, cost and risk with governance; adopt, or deviate with a formal, documented exception requested through governance
Known threat Treat in the risk register: avoid or mitigate (change design, process, scope; add controls), transfer financial loss (contract, indemnity, insurance) without assuming this creates compliance, escalate beyond your authority, accept only with approved documentation
Supplier obligations Put requirements in the contract (flow-down), require evidence and audit rights, and enforce them; stop affected work until a noncompliant supplier meets the requirement (Topic 22)
Rule change Reassess impact on scope and backlog, reprioritize by effective date and consequence, raise change requests (Topic 29)
Multinational projects Coordinate through program or portfolio governance; harmonize where possible and manage regional variations explicitly
Legal exposure Involve the legal team early; keep records; communicate carefully

No silent workarounds: a shortcut that bypasses an internal policy to meet a date needs a formal exception through governance, with risk analysis, not a private decision. Changes, even free improvements, go through change control.

8Use Methods to Support Compliance (ECO)

Method How it supports compliance
Governance framework and policies Define standards, approvals, escalation thresholds and responsibilities (Topic 12)
Compliance matrix or register Beyond PMBOK 8 Map each requirement to an owner, control, verification method, evidence and status; ties to the requirements traceability matrix
Requirements traceability Every requirement linked to deliverables, tests and acceptance criteria (Topic 15)
Definition of done and acceptance criteria Put tests, accessibility, security and compliance checks into each iteration or phase, not a final audit (Topic 18)
Checklists Confirm obligations at gates and handovers; keep them current
Audits and inspections Compliance audits or checklists against internal or external standards and benchmarks; quality audits are independent and constructive
Training and awareness Make people aware of requirements and policies; record attendance
Controls and approvals Segregate duties, require sign-offs, use automated checks where possible
Change and configuration control Keep approved versions controlled and findable; every change assessed for compliance impact
Controlled repository One accessible, versioned home for approved artifacts so auditors and stakeholders find the latest
Contract clauses and supplier audits Flow requirements down; verify them
Reviews and lessons learned Regular compliance reviews; update OPAs with what is learned
Standard data templates When a regulator requires a reporting format, standardize inputs at the source rather than remapping each period

9Measure the Extent to Which the Project Is Compliant (ECO)

PMBOK 8 checks: compliance audits or checklists against internal or external standards and benchmarks (Table 2-5); metrics that track compliance with corporate and legal policies; at closure, verify that all contractual, regulatory, legal, social and environmental obligations have been met; sustainability-related KPIs may sit in the scope statement, charter, business case or contracts, and compliance can be monitored in planning, execution and closure.

Indicator Beyond PMBOK 8examples What it shows
% of compliance requirements implemented and verified Coverage against the compliance register
Open audit findings (number, severity, age) and time to remediate Control effectiveness and responsiveness
Nonconformances or defects against standards Quality of compliance work
Permits, approvals and certifications obtained vs due Schedule risk to go-live
Training completion Awareness
Incidents and breaches (security, safety, environmental) Real-world failure
Supplier compliance rate Third-party risk
Sustainability KPIs (emissions, energy, waste) ESG obligations
Compliance cost vs plan Whether the effort is funded
  • Report to governance with a dashboard (red-amber-green with explanations for items outside threshold) and escalate findings that threaten mandatory requirements.
  • Repeat measurement at intervals; at closure confirm all obligations were met before accepting closure (Topic 35).

Compliance matrix statuses [Beyond PMBOK 8 — exam practice]: record for each requirement the control, the evidence and a status. Compliant = control in place and evidence available. Partially compliant = the control covers only part of the scope (for example a retention rule enforced in some systems but not others). Non-compliant = no control or no evidence. Not applicable = the requirement does not apply (for example a data-residency rule for a service that never stores data in that country), with the reason recorded. A waiver or deferral needs an approved decision through governance, not the project manager's own judgment.

10Predictive vs Agile vs Hybrid

Predictive Agile / adaptive Hybrid
Confirming requirements Up front in requirements documentation and traceability matrix Compliance items go into the backlog, prioritized by effective date and consequence; new rules reprioritize the backlog Fixed regulatory requirements in the baseline; others in the backlog
Verification Phase exit criteria, gate reviews, compliance audits Definition of done includes compliance checks every iteration; automated scans Gates for the regulated part, DoD inside iterations
Evidence Controlled repository, formal records Lightweight but traceable (tests, reviews, approvals in a shared repository) Both
Change Formal change control with compliance review Backlog changes with compliance in the acceptance criteria; contract thresholds respected Both
Regulated environments Often predictive with phase gates for regulators (healthcare, pharmaceuticals) Possible when regulatory evidence is built into the DoD Common

11Tailoring, Interactions and Checking Results

  • Tailor to the industry (heavily regulated work needs formal controls and gates), jurisdiction count, data sensitivity, contract terms, organization maturity, and use of new technology such as AI (privacy and legal limits).
  • PMBOK 8 examples: financial and pharmaceutical projects need formal controls (SOX, GDPR) and multi-phase tracking; a large multinational project must comply with varied regulations across agencies and countries, so governance integrates across domains and handles regional variation at program or portfolio level.
  • Interactions: quality (compliance is a quality dimension and quality requirement), risk (threats and consequences), procurement (supplier compliance, flow-down clauses), governance (policies, thresholds, escalation), stakeholders (regulators, auditors), change control, sustainability and closing (obligations verified).
  • Check results: the team knows governance structure, policies and standards and acts on them; internal and external auditing and customer governance requirements are understood; compliance audits or checklists are used; evidence is complete and accessible.

12Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

  1. A compliance requirement is a requirement: confirm it, plan it, verify it and evidence it. Releasing first and fixing later breaks the rule.
  2. Do not borrow: new product, substance, market or data type means confirm which rules apply.
  3. Classify and assign owners; unowned requirements are the ones that fail.
  4. Plan the verification method, not only the specification. How will compliance be demonstrated?
  5. Put compliance in the definition of done or exit criteria and test continuously, not in a final audit.
  6. Threats to compliance are risks; when they occur they are issues. Insurance transfers loss but does not create compliance.
  7. Mandatory means comply. Deadlines do not justify skipping a mandatory requirement; present consequences and schedule-safe alternatives to the sponsor.
  8. No silent workarounds or deviations: exceptions and waivers go through governance and are documented; free improvements still go through change control.
  9. Supplier compliance is your responsibility to enforce: flow requirements down by contract and verify them.
  10. Keep evidence findable: a controlled repository of approved artifacts; auditors should not have to hunt.
  11. A new rule or external change reshapes the backlog or scope (Topic 33); reassess early.
  12. Sponsor or customer requirements may be stricter than the law; customer-required sustainability criteria are quality requirements.
  13. Verify obligations at closure before closing the project.
  14. Report compliance with measurable indicators, not general assurances.
  15. Multinational projects: coordinate regional variations through program or portfolio governance.
  16. Do not ignore the human side: training and a speak-up culture are compliance controls; adoption suffers when compliance feels like a "tax", so connect it to value people care about (Topic 11).

13Exam Q&A

13.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1An optional industry standard for accessibility would add three weeks to the sprint plan, and the product team wants to skip it. The contract does not require it. What should the project manager do?

  • ASkip the standard, since it is voluntary and the contract does not require it
  • BPostpone the decision until a customer or regulator complains about accessibility
  • CAdopt the standard fully without asking anyone, to be on the safe side
  • DWeigh value, cost and risk with governance, then adopt it or document an exception
Show the answer

Answer: D. Voluntary standards are weighed for value, cost and risk with governance, which either adopts them or records a formal, documented exception. Skipping silently, adopting without approval or waiting for a complaint skips that decision.

S2Auditors ask the agile team to show that each regulatory requirement is implemented and verified, but the requirements are scattered across several documents. What would best support the team?

  • AA compliance matrix of requirements, owners, controls, verification and evidence
  • BA longer section in the project charter that lists all of the relevant regulations
  • CA weekly meeting at which the team states that it is complying with the rules
  • DA folder of every test result, sorted by the date on which each was created
Show the answer

Answer: A. A compliance matrix or register maps each requirement to its owner, control, verification method, evidence and status, tying into the traceability matrix. A charter paragraph, a date-sorted folder or verbal assurances do not show coverage.

S3A cloud subcontractor will process payment data for the project, but the contract contains no right to audit its controls. What should the project manager do?

  • ARely on the subcontractor's own statement that it meets the security standards
  • BAdd audit rights and evidence requirements to the agreement through change control
  • CCancel the subcontract and move the payment processing into the project team
  • DAccept the gap and record it as an assumption in the assumption log
Show the answer

Answer: B. Supplier obligations are enforced by putting requirements in the contract, with evidence and audit rights, and changing an agreement goes through change control. Relying on a statement, canceling outright or logging the gap as an assumption leaves the compliance unverified.

S4To save two weeks and 40,000 on a release, a sponsor suggests skipping a mandatory accessibility test, although a failure could bring fines of 500,000 and a stop-sale order. What should the project manager do?

  • AShow the consequences and offer schedule-safe alternatives
  • BRun the test but accept the fine in the budget as a cost of speed
  • CSkip the test and plan to run it after the deadline has passed
  • DAsk the testing laboratory to issue the certificate without running the test
Show the answer

Answer: A. For a mandatory requirement the question is how to comply, not whether, so the project manager analyzes the consequences of noncompliance, shows them to the sponsor and proposes alternatives that protect the schedule. Skipping the test, budgeting for fines or buying a certificate are breaches.

S5An agile rollout in five countries faces different data rules, and regional teams are making different choices about storage and consent. What is the best approach?

  • ACoordinate through program governance and manage regional variations
  • BChoose the home country's rules for every region to keep the project simple
  • CLet each region follow its own rules and report any problems at the end
  • DApply the strictest country's rules everywhere and ignore all regional differences
Show the answer

Answer: A. Multinational projects follow different regional rules, so variations are coordinated through program or portfolio governance, with harmonization where possible and explicit management of differences. Blanket strictest rules, regional isolation or home-country rules do not guarantee compliance in each jurisdiction.

S6The sponsor asks how compliant the project really is. Which set of indicators gives the most useful answer?

  • AThe number of compliance meetings held and hours of training delivered each month
  • BA statement from each team lead that no known breaches have occurred
  • CRequirements verified, open audit findings by age, and permits obtained
  • DThe count of regulations listed in the project's requirements document
Show the answer

Answer: C. Compliance is measured with indicators such as the share of requirements implemented and verified, open audit findings and their age, and permits obtained against due, reported to governance. Meeting counts, assurances and a list of regulations measure activity or awareness, not the extent of compliance.

S7To meet a go-live date, a hybrid project's team plans to skip the internal security review that policy requires and run it after launch. What should the project manager do?

  • ASkip the review and record the decision in the team's private notes
  • BStop the plan and seek a documented exception through governance
  • CRun a shorter version of the review and call it the full review
  • DAllow it, since the review will be completed shortly after the launch
Show the answer

Answer: B. Bypassing a policy to meet a date needs a formal exception granted through governance and supported by risk analysis, never a private decision. Postponing quietly, recording it privately or relabeling a shortened review are silent workarounds.

S8A team proposes buying insurance to cover fines for a known data-protection gap and treating the compliance risk as closed. What is the correct view?

  • AInsurance is not needed because fines are an unavoidable cost of doing business
  • BInsurance should be bought now and the gap fixed once the fines have been paid
  • CInsurance fully closes the risk, since the financial exposure has been covered
  • DInsurance transfers financial loss but does not create compliance, so fix the gap
Show the answer

Answer: D. Insurance can move financial loss, but it does not make the project compliant, so a known gap needs a response that reduces exposure, such as a fix or new controls. Treating the risk as closed, ignoring insurance or paying fines first misreads the purpose of the response.

S9Safety incidents on site keep occurring because new subcontractor staff were never told about the project's safety rules. Which method best supports compliance here?

  • AReplacing the subcontractor's staff after each incident that occurs
  • BA revised safety policy document sent by email to the subcontractor's office
  • CMore inspections by the project manager, with fines for each violation found
  • DTraining and awareness for everyone on site, with attendance recorded
Show the answer

Answer: D. Training and awareness make people familiar with requirements and policies, with attendance recorded as evidence. Penalties, a document emailed to an office or replacing staff do not ensure that the people on site know the rules.

S10The client has signed acceptance of a new plant, but the contract's environmental clause requires restoration of the construction site, which has not been done. What should the project manager do before closing?

  • AClose the project and hand the restoration to the operations team
  • BAsk the client to waive the clause verbally at the closing meeting
  • CComplete and verify the restoration obligation, then close the project
  • DClose the project, since the client has already accepted the plant
Show the answer

Answer: C. At closure the project verifies that all contractual, regulatory, legal, social and environmental obligations have been met, and client acceptance alone does not discharge them. Closing first, handing the duty off or seeking a verbal waiver leaves the obligation open.

13.2 Recall Q&As

R1Where do compliance requirements come from?

Show the answer

EEFs (legal restrictions, government or industry standards, public health and safety regulations), OPAs and policies, contracts, and sponsor, customer and sustainability commitments.

R2Which categories of compliance does the ECO name as examples?

Show the answer

Security, health and safety, sustainability and regulatory compliance. Other common categories: privacy, quality standards, financial reporting, contractual and policy or ethics.

R3What is a threat to compliance, and how is it treated?

Show the answer

A condition that could cause noncompliance; managed as a risk (owner, response) until it occurs, then as an issue.

R4Give examples of consequences of noncompliance.

Show the answer

Fines, legal action, stop-work orders, loss of license, contract termination, rework and delay, loss of market access, reputation damage, harm to people or the environment, project termination.

R5Name methods that support compliance.

Show the answer

Governance and policies, compliance matrix, traceability, definition of done, checklists, audits and inspections, training, controls and approvals, change and configuration control, controlled repository, contract clauses, reviews.

R6How do you measure compliance?

Show the answer

Indicators such as percent of requirements verified, open audit findings, nonconformances, permits obtained, training completion, incidents and supplier compliance, backed by audits or checklists against internal and external standards.

R7Who confirms compliance requirements?

Show the answer

The project manager with legal and compliance experts, subject matter experts, regulators and certifying bodies, confirmed with the sponsor and governance.

R8What should the approach decision consider?

Show the answer

Whether the requirement is mandatory or voluntary, the consequences of noncompliance, cost, risk, available options and the need for formal exceptions through governance.

R9What does Close Project or Phase verify about obligations?

Show the answer

That all contractual, regulatory, legal, social and environmental obligations have been met.

R10What is a compliance matrix?** **[Beyond PMBOK 8]

Show the answer

A table mapping each compliance requirement to an owner, control, verification method, evidence and status.

R11What is the governance domain's role in compliance?

Show the answer

Ensuring compliance with regulatory and legal requirements to maintain organizational accountability, and enforcing policies and standards.

R12How does quality assurance relate to compliance?

Show the answer

QA is about using processes effectively and following standards; related concepts are regulations, compliance and audits.

R13How is compliance handled in agile work?

Show the answer

Compliance items are prioritized in the backlog and checks are part of the definition of done in every iteration; new rules reprioritize the backlog.

R14How may governance be checked for compliance in predictive projects?

Show the answer

With compliance audits or checklists against internal or external standards and benchmarks.

14Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Sources EEFs (laws, standards, public health and safety), OPAs, contracts, sponsor and customer commitments
1. Confirm Identify what applies by jurisdiction, product, data and market; use legal experts; do not assume
2. Classify Legal, security and privacy, safety, environmental, quality, financial, contractual, policy; mandatory vs voluntary; owners
3. Threats Rule changes, project changes, suppliers, skills, shortcuts, evidence gaps, geopolitical, timing
4. Consequences Harm, stop-work, loss of license, fines, legal action, contract loss, rework, reputation, cancellation
5. Approach Mandatory: build in, plan verification; voluntary: governance decision; exceptions formal
6. Methods Policies, compliance matrix, traceability, DoD, checklists, audits, training, change control, repository
7. Measure % verified, open findings, nonconformances, permits, training, incidents, supplier compliance
Threats are... Risks until they occur, then issues
Insurance Transfers loss; does not create compliance
Agile Compliance in the backlog and DoD every iteration
Closure Verify contractual, regulatory, legal, social, environmental obligations
Multinational Program or portfolio governance manages regional variations
First-action pattern Confirm with experts, classify and assign owners, plan verification, escalate consequences, formal exceptions only, measure and report
